channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: What VCs Really Think About Personal AI Agents | E2347
gist: Menlo's Dee Doss guest-hosts a TWiST VC roundtable with Kanu Galadi (Khosla), Chris Farmer (SignalFire) and Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow) on OpenAI's math breakthroughs, whether value escapes frontier labs, AI data vendors, AI-native founders, and skepticism of Instinct's ~$10B personal-agent valuation versus incumbents like Meta's Muse. Also covers agents eroding friction-based business models, the Factory-Cognition spat, SaaS 'cigar butt' repricing, and FCC robotics sourcing rules.

themes.theme: AI math breakthroughs and where startup value survives

insights.claim: OpenAI's new math result, combined with its earlier Navier-Stokes work, means AI has made major progress on four of the six remaining unsolved Millennium Prize problems.
insights.speaker: Dee Doss (Menlo Ventures, guest host)
insights.so_what: Frontier-lab reasoning capability is compounding faster than consensus expects; reprice what remains defensible for startups.
insights.quote: major mathematical progress in four of the seven four of the six remaining unsolved biggest unsolved problems in mathematics with AI

insights.claim: Math is the first domain to fall because it is formal and verifiable; the investable wedge is startups that formalize messy natural-language domains (tax, financial code) so the same proof-style AI can operate on them.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: Back 'formalization layer' companies that turn tax/financial rules into machine-verifiable code and ride model improvements.
insights.quote: math happens to be a domain that is very formal and for AI to continue to build proofs on top of proofs is you can see why it's working

insights.claim: Finding early-stage investments whose value does not ultimately flow to the token generators (frontier labs) is getting harder and harder.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: Value capture is migrating to model providers; early-stage underwriting must explicitly test lab-absorption risk.
insights.quote: it is harder and getting harder and harder for all of us

insights.claim: Digital sciences will move fastest; the next wave is companies closing the loop with real-world wet-lab and robotic experiments in chemistry and physics.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: Lab-automation and closed-loop experimentation are the bottleneck plays for AI-for-science.

insights.claim: In AI-driven life sciences, capturing failed experiments matters because historically only successes entered clinical trials, while AI training needs the failures too.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Proprietary negative-result datasets are a defensible asset in bio-AI.
insights.quote: in an AI world, you want to capture all the failures as well

insights.claim: AI can design a cancer therapy or a better battery chemistry quickly, but proving safety in humans and manufacturing/testing remain the bottleneck, which is why physical AI is drawing so much investment.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Invest in the post-discovery validation and manufacturing steps that AI cannot compress.
insights.quote: AI can create a cancer therapy quickly. But I think there's still a lot in proving that it works safely in humans

insights.claim: Compute will eventually stop being the bottleneck: molecule creation that costs $50 million today might cost thousands of dollars in a few years, shifting the constraint to lab capacity, clinical trials, manufacturing and patents.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Long the physical throughput constraints (CROs, labs, manufacturing) as compute deflates.
insights.quote: something that costs $50 million to create you know a few years from now might be in the thousands of dollars

themes.theme: Compute moats vs context, data and new architectures

insights.claim: Frontier labs have the best compute efficiency (revenue per incremental compute dollar), creating an 'unfair balance of intelligence' versus startups with 5,000-10,000 GPUs.
insights.speaker: Dee Doss (Menlo Ventures, guest host)
insights.so_what: Startups competing head-on with labs on raw model capability face structural disadvantage.
insights.quote: it's a rich person's game

insights.claim: Models will not own everything: applying intelligence requires context, permissioning, guardrails and change management, which is why forward-deployed engineers have become such a thing.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: The wrapper layer (workflow, permissions, security, change management) remains a durable value pool.
insights.quote: I'm not at all a believer that the models are just going to own everything.

insights.claim: SignalFire flipped its portfolio mix from roughly 80% horizontal SaaS/ML to 80% vertical AI because vertical data density lets startups dramatically outperform general models lacking private context.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Vertical AI with proprietary data is a leading VC allocation shift.
insights.quote: we flipped to 80% vertical AI

insights.claim: EvenUp dominates personal-injury law AI because it has seen the cases and insurance negotiations, and 99% of that data is in the private domain, out of reach of big models.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Private-data verticals (legal claims, insurance) are hard for frontier labs to attack.
insights.quote: 99% of that data is in the private domain

insights.claim: Transformer models are still very inefficient in training data, training compute and serving compute, leaving room for algorithmic breakthroughs from outside the big labs, and LLMs/transformers will not be the only path to AGI.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: Fund efficiency and alternative-architecture research outside frontier labs.

insights.claim: If context windows expanded from about 1 million to 100 million tokens, the value of today's retrieval/context-engineering layers would change materially.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: Context-engineering startups carry obsolescence risk tied to long-context cost curves.
insights.quote: It's not limited to 1 million tokens as of today, but maybe 100 million

insights.claim: The current HBM shortage is driving efficiency innovation in open labs, and compute constraints will persist for about two to three years rather than five to seven.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: Compute/memory scarcity trade has a ~2-3 year horizon; plan for easing after.
insights.quote: probably for the next two to three years

insights.claim: Physical-world data collection creates flywheels labs ignore, e.g. weather-modeling company Windborne collects in-situ atmospheric data that will keep it ahead of others.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: Proprietary sensor-data networks are a defensible AI moat.

insights.claim: Per Vercel data, usage shifted from proprietary to open-weight models from roughly 80/20 to 20/80 within months, as enterprises build in-house skill to personalize models.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Pressure on proprietary model pricing; rising demand for enterprise fine-tuning/data services.
insights.quote: It went from like 8020 to 2080 in a matter of months

themes.theme: AI training-data vendors: durable or transient?

insights.claim: Per a Gokul tweet, the fastest company ever to reach a $1 billion revenue run rate is a data company selling to labs, but much of such revenue is non-recurring with variable margins.
insights.speaker: Dee Doss (Menlo Ventures, guest host)
insights.so_what: Headline growth in data vendors overstates quality of revenue.
insights.quote: the fastest company to go from uh zero to a billion in revenue run rate is actually not any of these guys that you've heard of it is actually a data company

insights.claim: SignalFire backs RL/data companies like Micro1, betting demand will migrate from a handful of labs to broader enterprises, though some revenue may fall as fast as it rose.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Data vendors' durability hinges on enterprise land-and-expand beyond lab concentration.

insights.claim: Khosla Ventures has avoided the AI data category entirely because labs eventually stop needing a given dataset and open-weight models distill from top labs, so terminal value may not exist.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: A top AI investor sees no terminal value in data-labeling/RL-environment vendors.
insights.quote: we haven't invested in anything in the data category for that reason

insights.claim: Data companies should be judged on gross profit, customer concentration and whether demand is structural; so far required expertise has risen as models improve, and they need little fixed capital, making them good cash generators even if little is proprietary.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Value data vendors like services businesses on gross profit, not ARR multiples.
insights.quote: even thinking about headline revenue is kind of like the wrong way to think about these businesses

insights.claim: A new class of mostly early-20s founders is scaling fast in accounting and legal categories without domain backgrounds, though vision, selling and recruiting remain the evergreen founder skills.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Domain expertise is less of a prerequisite in AI-native vertical software.

insights.claim: SignalFire invests bimodally: deep domain experts in some verticals and 'heat-seeking missile' young hackers with no industry knowledge, since outsiders reinvent industries during tectonic shifts.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Back outsider founders in categories undergoing AI disruption.
insights.quote: someone from telecom wasn't going to invent Snapchat or someone from the hotel industry wasn't going to invent Airbnb

insights.claim: Khosla is investing in a chip design company planning to release a chip with about 20 people because agents handle design exploration, RTL generation and physical design.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: AI agents collapse team size in capital-heavy domains like semis, changing capital efficiency.
insights.quote: release a chip with like 20 folks

insights.claim: Each technology generation widens outcome skew: the median gets slightly worse while the extremes get immensely powerful, e.g. a 19-year-old running 50 agents to break websites and collect bug bounties.
insights.speaker: Dee Doss (Menlo Ventures, guest host)
insights.so_what: Power-law in founder outcomes intensifies; concentrate on the extreme tail.
insights.quote: the median gets slightly worse, but the extremes get in immensely powerful

themes.theme: Personal AI agents: Muse, Instinct and incumbent advantage

insights.claim: Chris Farmer is a bear on Instinct's ~$10 billion valuation: incumbents with billions of users, Gmail/Apple data intimacy, ad networks and wallets have overwhelming advantages in getting trusted access to private data.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Avoid general personal-agent startups at high entry prices; incumbents favored unless specialized.
insights.quote: I'm a bear.

insights.claim: Startups can win personal agents only by specializing (e.g. travel) since users limit how many apps get access to sensitive data like SSNs and taxes.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Vertical consumer agents beat horizontal ones on trust.

insights.claim: OpenAI needed an ad network plus hardware to subsidize consumer agents, effectively rebuilding the Apple/Google stack, and Google is 'footfalling' despite it being Google's to lose.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Consumer AI monetization converges on ads; watch Google execution risk.

insights.claim: Instinct's $10B round was 'tail wagging the dog', forced by compute costs; underwriting requires believing it becomes a major consumer interface over OpenAI, Google, Meta or Apple.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Mega-rounds driven by compute needs inflate valuations beyond fundamentals.
insights.quote: I think it was a bit of like tail wagging the dog.

insights.claim: Muse is a phenomenal product reflected in Meta's stock price, while new agents (Hark, Sesame and others) launch constantly, creating 'personal agent fatigue' that favors whoever users onboard first.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Meta is a beneficiary of consumer agent adoption; late entrants face onboarding fatigue.
insights.quote: I actually have personal agent fatigue.

insights.claim: Instinct stored Sheil's credit card in plain text yet could pay a medical bill, while Muse only held tokenized card data and could not; he sees hundreds of millions, not a billion, of DAUs for personal agents.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Security vs capability trade-off is a live differentiator; size consumer agent TAM at hundreds of millions of DAU.
insights.quote: Instinct stored my credit card data in plain text

insights.claim: Personal agents could become the interface to everything digital, with stickiness from accumulated preferences; Kanu would back early bets (e.g. Rabbit, Vajjo's agent) but not a $10B entry price.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: Category large but entry price matters; early-stage agent bets preferred.
insights.quote: I would do that a 10 billion price as an entry point. I would be worried about that.

insights.claim: An agent identified Dee's eligibility for a €600 EU flight-delay refund and autonomously escalated with the airline to get it.
insights.speaker: Dee Doss (Menlo Ventures, guest host)
insights.so_what: Agents will drain 'breakage' revenue airlines rely on.
insights.quote: I'm eligible for a € 600 um uh refund

themes.theme: Agents remove friction: breakage business models at risk

insights.claim: Many business models depend on small amounts of friction; agents that automatically move credit card debt elsewhere could upend card interest economics.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Short friction-dependent revenue (card APR, breakage); long agent-native fintech.
insights.quote: so many business models are built on that little bit of friction preventing people from doing it

insights.claim: Systems built on breakage (airline refunds, insurance denials, rebates) will face relentless agents, forcing banks to compete harder on deposit rates as switching friction disappears.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Deposit beta and retention economics of banks deteriorate in an agent world.
insights.quote: banks will have to become more competitive on the interest rates that they pay

insights.claim: Chris Farmer is most bullish on personal finance and healthcare-admin agent use cases, and uses a self-built Claude personal operating system as chief of staff.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Admin-heavy domains (finance paperwork, insurance claims) are the highest-value agent use cases.

insights.claim: Agents don't search like humans: they can hit 800 links instead of one or two pages, so web infrastructure must be rebuilt for agents, as Parallel Systems is doing.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: Agent-native search/web infrastructure is a new category threatening human-centric search economics.
insights.quote: Agents can go to 800 of those links

insights.claim: Homogeneous agent decision-making across millions of users could create correlated behavior such as agent-driven bank runs or restaurant reservation crunches that systems weren't built for.
insights.speaker: Dee Doss (Menlo Ventures, guest host)
insights.so_what: Correlated agent behavior is a new systemic-risk vector for finance.
insights.quote: what if we have a bank run

themes.theme: VC conflicts, coopetition and SaaS repricing

insights.claim: The Factory vs Cognition public spat (including Vinod Khosla calling Factory second-tier despite investing) highlights that multi-stage funds now routinely hold competing companies, which may lead founders to refuse such investors again.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Investor conflicts in AI coding agents are rising; governance and information walls matter.

insights.claim: Menlo Ventures invested in Factory this week, a decision made before the public spat with Cognition broke.
insights.speaker: Dee Doss (Menlo Ventures, guest host)
insights.so_what: Signals continued institutional conviction in AI coding agents.
insights.quote: Menllo put some money into factory this week

insights.claim: Coopetition is pervasive: Nvidia sells to labs while competing on open weights, clouds compete on chips, and xAI leased tens of billions of dollars of data center capacity to Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Supplier/competitor lines blur; xAI capacity leasing shows compute monetization optionality.

insights.claim: Grokbot will use whichever underlying model is best for the use case, potentially Claude Opus or Codex, showing even model builders' products are model-agnostic.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: Model commoditization at the application layer pressures model pricing.

insights.claim: AI targets labor spend, an order of magnitude bigger than tech budgets, and makes vertical plays more investable than in the SaaS era when horizontal players like Salesforce dominated.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: TAM expansion favors AI companies capturing labor, especially vertical ones.
insights.quote: the spend on on labor tends to be or magnitude bigger than the spend on on tech budgets

insights.claim: Some SaaS businesses are 'cigar butts' that will disappear: seat-based pricing shrinks, interfaces get disintermediated and switching costs vanish because agents can do migrations.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Short seat-based SaaS with low differentiation; agent-driven migration erodes lock-in.
insights.quote: switching costs have gone away

insights.claim: Bending Spoons (acquirer of Miro and Airtable) acts like private equity, cutting costs and raising prices on legacy SaaS, while SaaS multiple compression also reflects unwinding of COVID-era 0% rates.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Legacy SaaS becomes a PE-style roll-up target; Figma shows quality SaaS still outperforms.

insights.claim: Traditional top-down SaaS follows 3-3-2-2-2 growth constrained by sales hiring, which looks slow next to consumption-priced AI businesses, causing sales talent to leave SaaS companies.
insights.speaker: Dee Doss (Menlo Ventures, guest host)
insights.so_what: Talent drain compounds SaaS growth disadvantage vs consumption AI models.

themes.theme: Regulation, politics and the seed-stage squeeze

insights.claim: FCC rules for compliant robot sales require 65% of the bill of materials to be sourced or licensed from US-friendly sources today, rising to 75% next year.
insights.speaker: Kanu Galadi (Khosla Ventures)
insights.so_what: Supply-chain localization requirements reshape robotics BOM and favor US-friendly suppliers.
insights.quote: today it's like 65% of the bomb needs to be sourced or licensed from US USfriendly next year is going to be 75

insights.claim: Physical AI will provoke visceral backlash: it's hard to choke GPT, but people can throw a beer bottle at a robot or a Waymo, making labor-layer AI highly political.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: Political/regulatory risk is a key underwriting factor for humanoid and robotaxi plays.
insights.quote: you can definitely throw a beer bottle at a at a at a robot

insights.claim: Capital intensity of AI (multi-billion-dollar data centers and chip buys) means venture investors must now understand Wall Street credit markets.
insights.speaker: Chris Farmer (SignalFire)
insights.so_what: AI infra financing ties venture outcomes to credit conditions.

insights.claim: Seed rounds are sometimes priced at $100 million-plus valuations in 2026, forcing seed funds to question whether diamonds in the rough remain and whether sub-$1B outcomes are acceptable.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: Seed valuation inflation compresses fund-level returns.
insights.quote: seed rounds are getting done at hund00 million plus valuations at times

insights.claim: Better Tomorrow ran a thesis on accounting, invested in three companies, and all have done quite well; it would do more in the category.
insights.speaker: Sheil Monat (Better Tomorrow Ventures)
insights.so_what: AI accounting is a validated seed thesis with appetite for more.
